chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Zarif al-Akfaani, who said:

A master gave permission to his slave to engage in buying and selling. The slave went bankrupt and a debt became incumbent upon him. He was taken for that debt which was upon him, but the value of the slave did not equal the debt upon him. He asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: 'If you sell him, the debt remains upon you; but if you emancipate him, the debt will not remain upon you.' So he emancipated him, and no debt remained upon him.
ai.seo_question: What happens to a slave's debt if the master emancipates him instead of selling him?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the financial liability of a master regarding a *mudabbarr* (slave granted freedom upon payment) or a slave with trading permission who incurs debt exceeding their value. The Imam distinguishes between two outcomes: selling the slave transfers the debt burden to the master for any shortfall, whereas emancipating the slave fully discharges the debt, relieving the master of all liability. This ruling highlights the strategic legal options available to masters in managing the financial risks associated with partially free slaves, emphasizing the merit of emancipation in clearing debts.
